findings.claim: Until the early 1990s, economists held a consensus that minimum wage increases had negative employment effects.
A 1982 review in the Journal of Economic Literature estimated that a 10% increase in the minimum wage reduced teenage employment by 1% to 3%.
Research by Card, Katz, and Krueger in the early 1990s found insignificant or negligible employment effects from minimum wage increases.
Economists currently disagree on the direction and magnitude of minimum wage impacts on employment.
Some research finds disemployment effects for young or unskilled workers with elasticities ranging from -0.1 to -0.3.
Meta-analyses have identified evidence of publication bias where studies finding statistically significant negative employment effects were more likely to be published.
Meta-regression analysis is used to model the effects of econometric specifications and study design heterogeneity on reported employment effects.
Card and Krueger (1994) used survey data on the number of workers to measure labor input.
Neumark and Wascher (1995, 1998) used payroll hours data to measure labor input.
Neumark and Wascher argue that Card and Krueger's results are influenced by the exclusion of federal minimum wage variation.
Neumark and Wascher contend that omitting federal minimum wage variation leads to an understatement of disemployment effects.
Critics of Neumark and Wascher argue that Neumark and Wascher used inadequate statistical controls to account for employment trends in the absence of a minimum wage increase.
Card and Krueger (2000) alleged that the administrative payroll data used by Neumark and Wascher (2000) suffered from selection bias.
Card and Krueger (2000) noted that the payroll data used by Neumark and Wascher was provided by a public affairs executive representing the food and beverage industry.
Neumark and Wascher argued that Card and Krueger's original findings were sensitive to the inclusion of average firm size as an instrument.
Neumark and Wascher (1992) estimated that a 10% increase in the minimum wage reduced teenage employment by 1–2%.
Neumark and Wascher (1992) estimated that a 10% increase in the minimum wage reduced young adult employment by 1.5–2%.
Card and Krueger (1994) found no adverse employment impact from the minimum wage increase in the New Jersey fast-food industry.
Neumark and Wascher (1998) argued that the decline in estimated disemployment effects is due to parameter instability.
The debate between Card and Krueger and Neumark and Wascher is cited as a methodological cautionary tale regarding study design and data selection.
An employer possesses monopsony power if the labor supply to their firm is not infinitely elastic.
Firms with monopsony power face an upward-sloping labor supply curve.
In a monopsonistic market, firms mark down wages below workers' marginal productivity.
A minimum wage can counteract monopsony power by relaxing labor supply constraints.
Minimum wage increases may initially boost employment by counteracting monopsony power.
Excessively high minimum wages can result in negative employment effects.
Some research finds larger positive employment effects from minimum wage increases when labor supply schedules are flatter.
Many difference-in-differences studies across U.S. states find no significant effect of minimum wages on employment.
In markets with high concentration, minimum wage elasticities of employment become more negative as the Kaitz Index intensifies.
Systematic empirical support for the monopsony argument is considered scarce by some researchers.
One study found that monopsony power does not have the predicted moderating effect on minimum wage employment responses.
Researchers distinguish between fluidity-based measures and concentration-based measures of monopsony power.
Failing to account for the interaction between city size and the minimum wage can bias elasticity estimates toward zero.
Quit elasticity is a common metric used to measure monopsony power.
Experimental and quasi-experimental variations in wages have yielded quit elasticities in the 2–3 range.
